lesson.menu_title: Inside the Workshop — Comparing Two Studies Out Loud
lesson.menu_desc: Saying which one is clearer, bigger or more useful, and why -- 32 slides
lesson.subtitle: Lesson 6 -- Inside the Workshop: Comparing Two Studies Out Loud
lesson.title_tag: Professor View -- Dejair Caitano do Nascimento | Lesson 6 -- Inside the Workshop

listenings.text: Good afternoon and welcome to the workshop. My name is Olga and I am facilitating this session. Before we start, three things about how this works. This is not a lecture. You are going to work in pairs, and every pair gets two studies to compare. Second, keep your answers brief. You have two minutes each, and the most common problem in this room is not silence, it is people who talk for eight minutes. Third, and this is the important one. I do not want you to tell me which study is better. I want you to tell me why. Better is easy. Why is the difficult part, and why is the reason we are here.

So, my pair and I looked at the two studies. The first one is much bigger, about four hundred patients, and the second one has only sixty. But bigger is not the same as more useful. The small study is far more detailed. They followed each patient for two years, they measured pain at home, not in the hospital, and their method is clearer than anything in the large study. For my own work, the smaller one is more relevant, because my patients also live far from the hospital. If somebody asks me which is the better study, I would say the large one. If somebody asks me which one I am going to use, it is the small one.
